description: X.509 certificate chains in COSE (RFC 9360). Each case signs a tag-44252 meter reading with a private key from the corpus, places a certificate chain in the protected header bucket, and then asks the implementation whether the message can be traced to a trust anchor. Both implementations do all of it, and each is then handed the other's message to validate — which is the only way to find out whether two DER parsers read the same certificate the same way. The corpus in cose-x509-corpus.json is minted by Bouncy Castle (tools/CertificateCorpus) and is deliberately not written by either party being tested: a parser checked against certificates its own package produced would agree with itself about any misreading. That argument holds for COSE.TS and not for Styx, whose parser is Bouncy Castle itself, so the certificates that are not DER live in cose-x509-messages.json, written by a third encoder. Every certificate is checked at the corpus's fixed validateAt, because a validity period tested against 'now' is a test that passes until it does not. The keys secure nothing.

cases.description: The case the whole feature exists for: a meter signs its reading with the brainpoolP256r1 key it was manufactured with, the message carries the meter certificate and the manufacturer's authority, and the recipient holds only the root. Note that the root is on P-256 and the authority beneath it on brainpoolP256r1 — the chain changes curve halfway down, which is what an implementation taking the curve from the certificate being checked rather than from the key checking it gets wrong.
The same chain with the root appended. RFC 9360 does not require the anchor to travel — the recipient has it already — but a sender that sends it anyway must not be penalised for it.

One certificate, which RFC 9360 spells as a bare byte string rather than an array of one — the array form starts at two. The certificate is also signed with Ed25519 rather than ECDSA, so what is being verified here is an EdDSA signature over a tbsCertificate, which is a different code path from an EdDSA signature over a Sig_structure.

A certificate signed with ML-DSA-65, which is where a certificate stops being small: 5458 octets of it, most of them the 3309-byte signature and the 1952-byte key. This is also the case no WebCrypto-based X.509 library can check at all, which is why the parsing and the verification here are this package's own.

The chain plus an x5t naming its end-entity certificate. A thumbprint is a name and never a reason to trust: it says which certificate the sender meant, so that a recipient who already holds it can find it.

The same thumbprint taken with SHA-384 instead of SHA-256. RFC 9360 Section 2 leaves the hash to the sender and makes the COSE_CertHash carry its identifier, which is the whole reason the identifier is there — and until this case the only algorithm any x5t vector named was SHA-256, so nothing held either side to reading the label rather than assuming it. An implementation that assumes computes 32 bytes where 48 travelled and refuses a sound message; one that writes 32 bytes under label -43 is refused by the other side for the same reason. cose-x509-messages Section 24 pins that the label must be a hash algorithm at all, with three that are not; this pins that a correct one other than the default is honoured.

The same with SHA-512, the widest hash either implementation offers for the purpose. Both algorithms are Recommended=Yes in the IANA COSE Algorithms registry and both were implemented on each side before any vector named them.

A sender demanding, through crit, that the chain actually be processed. The demand must be honoured by a verification that walks the chain and refused by one that does not — whoever verifies with a bare public key has looked at no certificate and must not claim otherwise.

The first chain here whose certificates are SIGNED with RSA rather than merely carrying an RSA key, which is a different question entirely: the signature on a certificate is what gets verified, so a chain signed with ECDSA says nothing about RSA however many RSA keys it certifies. This is the asymmetry the six algorithm rows of cose-sign uncovered rather than closed, recorded in FINDINGS Section 28 on 2026-11-03: Styx validated such a chain, because Bouncy Castle handles sha256WithRSAEncryption like anything else, and COSE.TS answered that "1.2.840.113549.1.1.11" is not a signature algorithm it knows. The count that found the other asymmetry never looked at this one, because it is in the other registry — the object identifiers of X.509 rather than the algorithms of COSE. Two certificates travel and both are verified: the meter's, signed with sha256WithRSAEncryption, and the manufacturer's authority above it, signed with sha384WithRSAEncryption by a root of 3072 bits. So one chain covers two of the three identifiers of RFC 4055 Section 5 and two signature widths, 256 octets and 384 — because the width of an RSA signature is the width of the signer's modulus, and an implementation that assumed one of them would pass every other certificate in this corpus. The meter signs the reading with RS256.

The same chain in the other scheme, and the one algorithm identifier in X.509 that does not say what it is. "PSS" is the identifier; the digest, the mask generation function, the length of the salt and the trailer field are written in the parameters beside it [RFC 4055, Section 3.1], which MUST be present for a signature and whose defaults are SHA-1 throughout. Both implementations therefore have to read a parameter set here rather than look up an identifier, and what this row measures is that two independent readings of those octets pick the same algorithm: the authority is signed with the SHA-384 parameter set and the meter with the SHA-256 one, and the meter signs the reading with PS256. Both sides accept only the shape RFC 8230 Section 2 fixes for the COSE PS* algorithms — MGF1 over the same hash, a salt as long as that hash — which is less a strictness than an arithmetic: a PSS verifier that takes the salt length from the hash cannot verify a signature that used another one, whatever it accepts.

The third identifier of RFC 4055 Section 5, and the crossing: this certificate is signed with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and SHA-512, and the meter beneath it signs the reading with RSASSA-PSS. The two layers have nothing to do with one another — a certificate certifies a key and says nothing about what the key will be asked to do — and an implementation that read the message's algorithm off the certificate it arrived with, or the certificate's off the message, would still pass the two rows above, where the two happen to agree. It is also the row where an RSA key does both jobs in one message: verifying 256 octets of certificate signature with the authority's key, and 256 octets of message signature with the key the certificate carries.

The mirror of the row above: a certificate signed with the widest RSASSA-PSS parameter set over a message signed with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5. It completes the six forms — three identifiers of RFC 4055 Section 5 and three parameter sets of its Section 3.1, each one verified by both implementations. The widest set is also where the padding nearly runs out: 64 octets of digest, 64 of salt, eight zero octets and a trailer leave 126 of the 256 octets of the encoded block, and in a 1024-bit modulus it would not fit at all. Which is one way of reading the key size RFC 8230 Section 6.1 requires: the widest of these algorithms has no room in a narrow key.
A chain that is internally perfect and leads somewhere the recipient has never heard of. This is the ordinary failure and the one that must not be confused with a broken signature.
An end-entity certificate whose validity ended in 2021, checked at the corpus's fixed instant in 2026.
The other end of the same check, which implementations forget far more often than expiry: a certificate whose validity has not begun.

A certificate issued by something whose basic constraints say it is not an authority. Every signature in this chain is valid; the chain is still not one, because a leaf certificate that can mint further certificates makes its issuer's policy meaningless.
A certificate whose key usage permits key encipherment and not digital signatures, used to sign. The chain is impeccable and the certified key says it is not for this.
Two certificates from two different hierarchies, put one after the other. The link between them does not hold, whichever anchor is offered.

The failure a chain check alone never catches, and the reason validating a chain and verifying a signature must never be two separate answers: the chain is valid, leads to the trusted root, and certifies a key that did not sign this message. An implementation that reported the chain's subject as the signer here would be naming the wrong meter, with every certificate in order.

An x5t naming a certificate other than the one that travelled. One of the two statements is wrong and there is no way to tell which, so the message is refused rather than resolved in favour of either.
